pages.title: One warming effect, two routes

blocks.text: Water can warm when placed on a hot plate or when stirred by a paddle in an insulated vessel. The same temperature rise can be reached through different transfers. We need a rule that counts both without treating either as a substance stored in water.

Heat q is energy transferred because of a temperature difference. Work w is energy transferred by other organised means, such as a force moving a piston. Internal energy U is a property of the system; q and w describe a process.

pages.transition: The energy account becomes a conservation equation.

pages.title: The first law is an energy balance

blocks.text: For a closed system, ΔU = q + w. The first law states that energy is conserved: any change in internal energy is accounted for by heat and work exchanged. Use the same energy units for all three quantities.

Energy entering as heat or work increases the account; energy leaving decreases it. There is no additional energy created merely because a chemical reaction releases heat. Energy is transferred while the system changes its state.
Closed means no matter crosses the boundary. Energy carried by incoming or outgoing matter would need an additional accounting term for an open system.

pages.transition: A consistent sign convention makes the balance usable.

pages.title: Read the signs from the system perspective

blocks.text: Heat absorbed by the system: q > 0. Heat released: q < 0. Work done on the system: w > 0. Work done by the system: w < 0. These are the chemistry sign conventions used in ΔU = q + w.

Compressing a gas transfers work to it, so w is positive. Expanding against a resisting external pressure transfers work to the surroundings, so w is negative. A cooling sample generally releases heat, so its q is negative.
Do not change conventions halfway through a problem. The phrase work done by the gas gives the direction of transfer, not a positive sign in this convention.

pages.transition: Follow a complete balance with both heat and work present.

pages.title: Worked balance: some supplied heat leaves as work

blocks.text: Teacher-created example: a gas absorbs 500 J and does 200 J of work on its surroundings. Given q = +500 J and w = −200 J. Find ΔU. Select ΔU = q + w; substitute ΔU = 500 + (−200) = +300 J. The system keeps 300 J as increased internal energy.

The heat input is not equal to ΔU because some energy is transferred out as work. This distinction is why a reaction energy and the measured heat are not interchangeable without stating the experimental conditions.

pages.transition: The same initial and final states can have different separate heat and work values.

pages.title: State function versus path function

blocks.text: A path function depends on how a process is performed. q and w are path-dependent, while their sum ΔU depends only on the initial and final states. A system therefore does not possess an amount of heat or work as a state property.

Suppose route A has q = +100 J and w = +50 J, giving ΔU = +150 J. Route B between the same states delivers 30 J of work, so w = −30 J. Its required heat is q = ΔU − w = 150 − (−30) = +180 J. The energy change is identical despite different transfers.

pages.transition: An isolated system is the simplest limiting case of this balance.

pages.title: Check the boundary conditions first

blocks.text: In an isolated system, q = 0 and w = 0, so ΔU = 0. In a closed adiabatic process, q = 0 but work may occur, giving ΔU = w. Neither statement requires U itself to be zero.

A sealed insulated rigid container, with no electrical or other work crossing its boundary, approximates an isolated system. Internal changes can redistribute its energy even though total U remains constant.
Constant internal energy does not prove nothing happens. A chemical change can redistribute energy among microscopic forms inside an isolated system.

pages.transition: For many gas experiments, work comes from moving the boundary.

pages.title: Why a piston transfers energy

blocks.text: A gas expanding in a cylinder pushes a piston against an external force. The piston moves a distance, so energy is transferred mechanically. During compression, the surroundings push the piston inward and transfer energy to the gas.

If the piston area is A and the opposing external pressure is p(ex), the force is p(ex)A. A displacement changes volume by A times distance, leading to the pressure–volume work expression. Pressure is force per unit area.
The gas pressure helps determine whether the piston moves, but the resisting external pressure determines the work transferred to the surroundings.

pages.transition: This force–distance argument gives a useful work formula.

pages.title: Pressure–volume work at constant external pressure

blocks.text: For constant external pressure, w = −p(ex)ΔV = −p(ex)[V(final) − V(initial)]. Expansion gives ΔV > 0 and w < 0; compression gives ΔV < 0 and w > 0. Pressure in Pa and volume in m³ give work in J.

Unit checks: 1 Pa m³ = 1 J; 1 L bar = 100 J; 1 L atm = 101.325 J. Use the conversion matching the pressure unit supplied. These conversions prevent an answer numerically correct in L bar from being mislabelled as J.

pages.transition: Use the external pressure and then put the work into the first law.

pages.title: Worked piston problem

blocks.text: Teacher-created example: a gas expands from 2.0 L to 5.0 L against 1.0 bar and absorbs 600 J. Find w and ΔU. ΔV = 5.0 − 2.0 = 3.0 L. Then w = −1.0 × 3.0 = −3.0 L bar = −300 J. Finally ΔU = 600 − 300 = +300 J.

The gas transfers 300 J as work while receiving 600 J as heat. The remaining 300 J increases its internal energy. Had the external pressure been different, the work could change even for the same volume endpoints.
Subtract final minus initial volume before assigning the sign. Writing a negative ΔV for expansion and also adding the formula minus sign reverses the physical meaning.

pages.transition: Revise the system-based sign convention before adding reversible paths.

pages.title: Revision: conserve energy and label the path

blocks.text: The first law for a closed system is ΔU = q + w. U depends on state; heat and work depend on the process. Heat entering and work done on the system are positive. Heat leaving and work done by the system are negative.

For constant external pressure, w = −p(ex)ΔV. Check the pressure–volume energy conversion. Isolation gives ΔU = 0, while adiabatic only sets q = 0. Always state whether mechanical, electrical or other work is possible.

questions.question: A gas releases 250 J and receives 100 J of work. Find ΔU.
questions.answer: q = −250 J and w = +100 J, so ΔU = −150 J. The system loses internal energy.

questions.question: Why are heat and internal energy different quantities?
questions.answer: Heat measures energy transferred due to a temperature difference during a process. Internal energy is a state property, and can also change through work.

questions.question: A gas compresses by 2 L against 1 bar. What is the work?
questions.answer: ΔV = −2 L, so w = −1 × (−2) = +2 L bar = +200 J. Compression transfers energy to the gas.

questions.question: Can q differ between paths with the same ΔU?
questions.answer: Yes. Work can also differ, provided q + w remains the same endpoint energy change.

questions.question: Does a rigid sealed vessel automatically make q zero?
questions.answer: No. Rigidity sets ΔV = 0 and removes pressure–volume work. Heat may still cross a conducting wall.

title: The First Law and Pressure–Volume Work
